title: The cathedral labyrinth
hookLine: at Chartres, pilgrims walk a winding path to the center as a prayer
carry: the long way is the way
last: FEATHER ON THE BREATH OF GOD.

lines: A CIRCLE SET IN THE STONE FLOOR.
cards: Stand in the nave of Chartres Cathedral, in France, and look down. Set into the stone floor is a great circle: one winding path, dark lines curving around a flower-shaped center.
When it's open for walking, people step onto it one after another and begin. No one is meant to race. No one is meant to cut across.
The path swings toward the center, then away again, out toward the edge, then back, until it seems you'll never get there. And then you do.

teach.h: A LABYRINTH IS NOT A MAZE.
teach.b: First, a labyrinth isn't a maze. A maze is a puzzle, built to trick you, full of dead ends and wrong turns. A labyrinth has one path.
You can't get lost in it; you only have to keep walking. On the Chartres floor the path brings you close to the center, then swings you all the way out to the edge, then back, again and again.

teach.h: THE WAY IN FEELS LIKE THE WRONG WAY.
teach.b: The way in feels like the wrong way, and it isn't. It's the only way there is. How did medieval Christians use it?

The floor itself doesn't say. Some readers suggest pilgrims walked it as a pilgrimage in miniature, a journey to Jerusalem on a cathedral floor. That's a story often told, and historians aren't certain of it.
What's clear is how people use it now: slowly, as a prayer with the feet.
Some walkers think of it as a journey with stages: going in, letting things go; resting at the center; coming out, carrying something back into the world. Scripture gives the walk its words.
The letter to the Hebrews says the people of faith "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." A pilgrim is someone on the way, not yet home.

And a psalm, in the King James words: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for the feet lights the next step, not the whole road. The labyrinth teaches the same thing in stone.
You never need to see the center. You only need the next turn.

how: Some churches and retreat centers have labyrinths on the floor or the grounds, and people walk them slowly as a form of prayer or reflection, sometimes at set times when the path is cleared.

games.q: you're walking the labyrinth, and the path suddenly swings you back out to the edge, far from the center. what do you do?
o: step across the lines to the center.
games.why: there's only one path, and it does reach the center. the stretch that seems to lead away is part of the way in.

practice: If you can stand, walk a wide, slow circle that tightens toward a center point, pause there, then turn and unwind it back out, in small steps.

If you pray, carry a name or a worry in, set it down at the center, and walk out without it. If you can't stand or walk right now, trace a spiral with one finger on your palm or a table, in and out, as slowly as you can.

wordCard.voice: Cathedral labyrinth. One winding path set in a church floor, walked slowly as a prayer, with no dead ends and no shortcuts.

carryVoice: Your line: the long way is the way. No dead ends, only turns. Until tomorrow.
